scenes.desc: La gira de los Ramones de 1976 contagia a Inglaterra, donde el punk es combinación de moda y paro: la Gran Bretaña de Thatcher, con las ciudades industriales devastadas, convierte el «punk» en algo mucho más serio que lo que pretendían los Ramones. Malcolm McLaren inventa el sonido (Sex Pistols, «los Ramones con heroína y valium») y la imagen. The Clash, los más intelectuales (London Calling, Sandinista); Damned, Generation X, Buzzcocks (inventores del punk-pop), Vibrators. En Australia, Radio Birdman y los Saints. La segunda ola (GBH, UK Subs, Neurotics, New Model Army, Stiff Little Fingers) y el punk anarquista (Crass, Discharge, Rudimentari Peni, Subhumans).

mentions.text: …Damned (1977) was the quintessence of British punk-rock, even though with Black Album (1980) they converted to melodic hard-rock. Billy Idol's Generation X (1), were also unique in that they did pay attention to melody: their songs were actually hummable and Generation X (1978) was actually musical. The Buzzcocks were even more melodic (beating the Ramones at their own game) and virtually invented punk-pop with…

podcast.title: Billy Idol Witnesses The Ramones (July 4, 1976)
podcast.body: A "very young Billy Isle" (Idol), then part of Generation X, was present at The Ramones' influential gig at the Roundhouse in London on July 4, 1976. He was among the many future British punk figures who were "transformed by what they saw and heard." "Generation X featuring a very young Billy Isle. They were all at these gigs and they were all transformed by what they saw and heard."

podcast.title: Influenced by The Ramones
podcast.body: Generation X, founded by Billy Idol, was profoundly influenced by The Ramones after seeing them perform in England in 1976. Billy Idol found The Ramones "brilliant," and their style impacted how his own band chose to play. "a punk band called Generation X Which was started by someone called Billy Idol saw them play Billy Idol said he thought they were brilliant and it influenced how his band chose to play."

podcast.title: Recording at Wessex Studios
podcast.body: Generation X recorded at Wessex Studios, an old church hall in North London that attracted many punk and post-punk bands for its distinctive live sound. "A lot of punk bands and post punk bands, like using the place, the clash and the damned and suzy and the banshees and the pretenders and the specials and generation X and the sex pistols."

concerts.title: The Roundhouse (July 4th, 1976, London)
concerts.body: Generation X, featuring a "very young Billy Idol," was present at this Ramones gig, one of two shows that profoundly transformed major players in the British punk rock explosion. "Generation X featuring a very young Billy Idol."

xref.title: Conquest of England (July 4 & 6, 1976)
xref.body: The Ramones played two pivotal shows in London, first at the Roundhouse (capacity 2,000) on America's bicentennial, and then at Dingwalls two nights later. Despite their European record company trying to cancel gigs, the band delivered explosive performances. These concerts were England's "first proper exposure" to US-style punk rock and are credited with transforming nearly every major player in the burgeoning British punk rock scene, including members of the Sex Pistols, The Clash, The Pretenders, The Damned, and Generation X. "And over the course of those two nights, July 4th and July 6th, 1976, just about every single person who would become a major player in the British punk rock explosion were taught a lesson by the Ramones."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Witnessing The Ramones (July 4, 1976)
xref.body: Members of the newly formed Clash, including Joe Strummer, were present at The Ramones' July 4, 1976 gig at the Roundhouse in London. Strummer recounted how they got backstage by forming a "human chain" through a window to meet The Ramones, describing it as a "really great punk rock moment." "Members of the newly formed clash, Chrissy Hind of the still unformed pretenders, the damn who would become the first British punk band to release a record, Generation X featuring a very young Billy Isle. They were all at these gigs and they were all transformed by what they saw and heard."

xref.title: Origin from Aberdeen, Washington
xref.body: Nirvana emerged from Aberdeen, Washington, as an initially unknown band. Their rise to prominence symbolized the shift where Generation X began to define the course of rock and roll, taking over from the influences of the Baby Boomers. "And that spark ended up coming from an unknown band from Aberdeen, Washington."

xref.title: Pop Dominance in Early 1990s
xref.body: Milli Vanilli contributed to the pop music sound that ruled at the very beginning of the 1990s, before a series of events and the rise of Generation X ushered in the era of grunge and alternative music. "At the very beginning of the decade, pop music ruled Michael Jackson, Janet Jackson, Maddon, Millie Vanilley, and new kids on the block."

xref.title: Punk Scene Roots
xref.body: Born William Broad, Billy Idol was deeply immersed in the original punk rock scene, actively following the Sex Pistols and associating with seminal figures like Johnny Rotten and Sid Vicious before adopting his stage name and forming Generation X. "William Broad followed the pistols everywhere. He was deep into the original punk rock scene."

xref.title: Rise of Alternative Rock
xref.body: Pearl Jam was among the many bands that saw a massive increase in record sales and broader recognition following the breakthrough success of Nirvana's *Nevermind* in 1991. They were part of a wave of "formerly fringe acts" that capitalized on Generation X's growing appetite for alternative music. "More jam, Soundgarden, Smashing Pumpkins, Stone Table Pile, Chili Peppers, and dozens and dozens of other formerly friendjacks started selling records and contradictions by the boatload."

xref.title: Strategic Single Release and Unforeseen Success
xref.body: On August 27, 1991, an advanced single (likely "Smells Like Teen Spirit") was sent to alternative radio stations, not as the band's or label's first choice, but as a marketing tactic to "break the ice with the freaks." Expectations for the album were so low that selling 100,000 copies would have been thrilling, with only 46,251 copies initially manufactured for stores. However, the song's radio debut caused an explosion of listener demand, leading to immediate sell-outs and rapid weekly sales of 300,000 copies within two months, demonstrating the sudden mobilization of Generation X. "expectations were really low. If this album eventually sold 100,000 copies, everybody, including the band, would be thrilled."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Terry Chimes' Career Change to Healthcare
xref.body: After a successful music career with The Clash, Generation X, and Black Sabbath, Terry Chimes began to rethink his path in the late 1980s. Influenced by his experiences with the rock and roll lifestyle, he concluded that "the natural way of healing is far better than pumping people full of drugs." This led him to adopt a meat- and alcohol-free lifestyle, study chiropractic medicine at various schools across the UK, and learn acupuncture in China. "But by the end of the 1980s, Terry began thinking about doing something else."

xref.title: Unexpected Global Phenomenon
xref.body: Nirvana's transformation from an unknown cult band from Aberdeen, Washington, into one of the biggest and most important bands in rock history was an "fabulous artistic, economic, demographic, and sociological question." Their rise coincided with Generation X's disillusionment, a recession, and a desire for authentic, anti-star musicians. "But we have to ask, how did this unknown cult band from nowhere Washington suddenly become not only one of the biggest bands in the world, but also one of the most important in the history of rock?"
